content: Oritavancin is an antibiotic used to treat acute bacterial skin and skin structure infections. It is administered as a single 1200 mg intravenous dose. There are two available products, Orbactiv and Kimyrsa, which differ in dose strengths, infusion duration, reconstitution and dilution instructions, and compatible diluents. The safety and efficacy of oritavancin in patients under 18 years of age have not been established. Coadministration of oritavancin with the cholera vaccine should be avoided due to pharmacodynamic antagonism, as systemic antibiotics may inactivate the vaccine strain. Patients who have received oral or parenteral antibiotics within 14 days prior to cholera vaccination should not receive the vaccine. Similarly, oritavancin may reduce the efficacy of oral microbiota products containing bacterial spores. Antibiotic regimens should be completed 2–4 days before initiating oral microbiota therapy. Oritavancin interacts with several drugs by affecting hepatic and intestinal enzyme metabolism, particularly CYP3A4, CYP2D6, CYP2C9, and CYP2C19. It may decrease the levels or effects of drugs such as carbamazepine, clonidine, disopyramide, ethosuximide, flecainide, quinidine, quinine, sirolimus, and tacrolimus. Conversely, it may increase the levels or effects of drugs like fosphenytoin, phenobarbital, phenytoin, primidone, and valproic acid. Caution and close monitoring are advised when coadministering oritavancin with drugs that have a narrow therapeutic index. Oritavancin is contraindicated in patients with hypersensitivity to the drug or other glycopeptides (e.g., vancomycin, dalbavancin, telavancin). Hypersensitivity reactions, including anaphylaxis, have been reported. Infusion-related reactions resembling Red-Man Syndrome (e.g., flushing, urticaria, pruritus, rash) may occur and can be managed by slowing or interrupting the infusion. Other infusion reactions, such as chest pain, back pain, chills, and tremors, have also been observed. The safety of administering more than one dose during a single course of therapy has not been established. In clinical trials, oritavancin was associated with a higher incidence of osteomyelitis compared to vancomycin. If osteomyelitis is suspected, appropriate alternative antibacterial therapy should be initiated. To minimize the development of drug-resistant bacteria, oritavancin should only be used for infections proven or strongly suspected to be caused by susceptible bacteria. There is no available data on the use of oritavancin in pregnant women to assess the risk of major birth defects, miscarriage, or adverse maternal or fetal outcomes. While it is unknown if oritavancin is excreted in human milk, it has been detected in the milk of rats. The benefits of breastfeeding should be weighed against the mother’s clinical need for the drug and potential adverse effects on the breastfed child. Oritavancin may interfere with certain laboratory tests, including blood clotting tests (e.g., PT, INR, aPTT), potentially causing false results. Patients should inform their healthcare provider about all medications and supplements they are taking to avoid potential drug interactions. Prolonged or repeated use of oritavancin may lead to oral thrush or new yeast infections. Rarely, it may cause a severe intestinal condition due to Clostridioides difficile (C. difficile), which can occur during or weeks to months after treatment. Patients experiencing serious symptoms of overdose, such as loss of consciousness or difficulty breathing, should seek emergency medical attention. Routine laboratory tests, such as liver function tests, may be performed during treatment. Unopened vials of oritavancin should be stored at 20–25°C (68–77°F), with excursions permitted between 15–30°C (59–86°F).
